To determine whether the proposed solution is correct, let us evaluate the integral:

$$\int_{-9}^{11} f(u) \, \mathrm{d}u$$

Let $u = p(x) = x^7 + 6x^5 + 3x^3 + 1$. Then:
- When $x = -1$, $p(-1) = -1 - 6 - 3 + 1 = -9$.
- When $x = 1$, $p(1) = 1 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 11$.
- $\mathrm{d}u = p'(x) \, \mathrm{d}x = (7x^6 + 30x^4 + 9x^2) \, \mathrm{d}x$.

Using the substitution $u = p(x)$:
$$\int_{-9}^{11} f(u) \, \mathrm{d}u = \int_{-1}^{1} f(p(x)) p'(x) \, \mathrm{d}x = \int_{-1}^{1} (9x + 5)(7x^6 + 30x^4 + 9x^2) \, \mathrm{d}x$$

Expanding the integrand:
- The term $9x(7x^6 + 30x^4 + 9x^2)$ is an odd function, so its integral over $[-1, 1]$ is $0$.
- The term $5(7x^6 + 30x^4 + 9x^2)$ is an even function, so:

$$\int_{-1}^{1} 5(7x^6 + 30x^4 + 9x^2) \, \mathrm{d}x = 5 \left[ x^7 + 6x^5 + 3x^3 \right]_{-1}^{1} = 5 \times (10 - (-10)) = 100$$

The proposed solution omitted the derivative factor $\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}v} = p'(v)$ during the substitution (incorrectly setting $\mathrm{d}u = \mathrm{d}v$), leading to the incorrect result of $10$ instead of $100$.

VERDICT: REJECT
